In a session

He pays attention to what changes.

Garrett watches how you move, then builds an exact physical setup around what is happening in your body that day. You are active throughout: moving, breathing, engaging, and noticing.

His hands, timing, and instructions make small adjustments possible. The point is not to give you a theory about your body. It is to see whether the work changes something you can feel.

Named for a boy who inspired change.

Garrett felt an immediate connection to Amari, a boy he never met. Both faced life-threatening complications from asthma at the same age; Garrett survived, while Amari did not. The name gives the work a deeper purpose: helping people experience more of their own physical capacity through patient, individual guidance.

What makes the Amari Method different.

  1. 01

    The work is physical and specific.

    Position, leverage, breath, engagement, touch, and support all matter. Garrett changes the setup until the body has a different option.

  2. 02

    Sessions are dynamic.

    You may work on the floor, standing, with rings, blocks, rollers, or nothing at all. The room is used to create the right physical conditions, not to run everyone through the same routine.

  3. 03

    You are active in the change.

    You are not placed on a table and worked on. You move, breathe, and participate while Garrett gives direct, hands-on guidance.

  4. 04

    The practice can become yours.

    A longer practice is teacher-led, not a fixed curriculum. Living Practice helps you revisit the visual cues of work you have already learned between sessions.
